title: The discount-price arm shows higher revenue per session in the logs — roll it out everywhere?

scenario.role: You're the pricing analyst at Redbrick Market
scenario.situation: A live pricing bandit has been leaning toward showing the aggressive-discount arm to customers with a high predicted lifetime-value score — a "protect our best customers with a deal" heuristic the pricing team added mid-flight. Looking at the logs, Farah, the pricing lead, sees the discount arm earns $14 more revenue per session on average than standard pricing, and wants to roll the discount out to all traffic.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "The discount arm earns $14 more per session in the logs. It's clearly driving more revenue — let's roll it out everywhere."
scenario.question: Was the discount arm shown to a representative mix of customers, or did the LTV-based targeting skew who saw it? Estimate the discount arm's real effect on revenue per session — correcting for who actually got shown each arm — before rolling it out everywhere.

columns.name: customer_ltv_score
columns.description: Pre-existing predicted lifetime-value score for this customer (0-100), computed before this session

columns.name: arm
columns.description: aggressive_discount or standard_price — which pricing this session was shown

columns.name: propensity
columns.description: The logging policy's probability of showing THIS session the arm it actually got, given customer_ltv_score

columns.name: revenue_per_session
columns.description: Revenue generated in this session, in dollars — the reward

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Farah's number: mean revenue_per_session for arm == aggressive_discount versus standard_price. How big is the naive gap?
Compare mean customer_ltv_score between the two arms. Were both arms shown to a similar mix of customers?
If the bandit preferentially showed the discount arm to high-LTV customers, what does that do to a raw average-revenue comparison — even if the discount itself hurt revenue?
Use the propensity column to inverse-weight each session (weight = 1/propensity) and recompute each arm's average revenue. What happens to the gap — does it just shrink, or does it flip sign?
Would you recommend rolling the discount out to all traffic based on the honest, propensity-corrected number?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the naive gap: mean(revenue_per_session) for aggressive_discount minus standard_price.
Profile who saw each arm: compare mean customer_ltv_score between the two arms.

Name the mechanism: the logging policy assigned the discount arm more often to high-LTV customers (who spend more regardless of pricing), so a raw average blends the arm's effect with a large pre-existing LTV difference.
Compute the inverse-propensity-weighted (Hajek/self-normalized) revenue for each arm: weight each arm's sessions by 1/propensity and take a weighted average.
Compare the honest, propensity-corrected gap to the naive one — check the sign, not just the size — and translate that into a rollout recommendation.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the naive gap, see who each arm was shown to, then re-weight the logs so the comparison is fair.

cells.title: Reproduce the naive gap
cells.explain: Mean revenue per session for the discount arm against standard pricing, straight from the logs.
cells.code:
means = df.groupby("arm")["revenue_per_session"].mean()
naive_gap = means["aggressive_discount"] - means["standard_price"]
print(f"naive gap: {naive_gap:+.2f} per session")
means.round(3)
cells.reads: Read off the logs, the discount arm looks clearly better. These logs were not a randomised test.

cells.title: Profile who saw each arm
cells.explain: The logging policy chose which sessions saw which price. Compare customer value across the arms.
cells.reads: The discount arm was shown far more often to high-LTV customers, who spend more whatever price they see.

cells.title: See the assignment rule in the propensities
cells.explain: propensity records how likely each session was to get the arm it got. Look at how it moves with customer value.
cells.code:
df["ltv_band"] = pd.qcut(df["customer_ltv_score"], 5, labels=False, duplicates="drop")
by_band = df.groupby(["ltv_band", "arm"]).size().unstack()
by_band = by_band.div(by_band.sum(axis=1), axis=0) * 100
print("share of sessions by arm, within each LTV band (%)")
by_band.round(1)
cells.reads: Arm assignment tracks customer value directly. That is the bias the raw average is absorbing.

cells.title: Re-weight by inverse propensity
cells.explain: Weight each session by 1 over its propensity and take a self-normalised (Hajek) average, so over-represented sessions stop dominating.
cells.code:
df["ipw"] = 1 / df["propensity"]
def hajek(group):
    return (group["revenue_per_session"] * group["ipw"]).sum() / group["ipw"].sum()
corrected = df.groupby("arm").apply(hajek)
corrected_gap = corrected["aggressive_discount"] - corrected["standard_price"]
print(f"propensity-corrected gap: {corrected_gap:+.2f} per session")
corrected.round(3)
cells.reads: Once each session is weighted by how likely it was to be there, the arms look very different.

cells.title: Put the two gaps side by side
cells.explain: The number the logs suggest, against the number a fair comparison supports. Watch the sign.
cells.code:
pd.DataFrame(
    {"gap per session": [naive_gap, corrected_gap]},
    index=["naive log average", "inverse-propensity weighted"],
).round(3)
cells.reads: Rolling out the discount on the naive number would roll out a price cut whose apparent gain belonged to the customers, not the price.

teachingNote.naiveRead: The discount arm earns about $14 more revenue per session than standard pricing in the raw logs. Read directly, that's a strong, obvious case to roll the discount out to everyone.
teachingNote.theTrap: The bandit's logging policy wasn't neutral: it leaned toward showing the discount arm to customers with a high predicted LTV score (a "protect our best customers" heuristic added mid-flight), and LTV score is a strong predictor of revenue per session on its own, regardless of pricing. Discount-arm sessions average an LTV score of 58.6 versus 42.9 for standard pricing — a large pre-existing gap. Comparing raw average revenue between arms therefore compares an already-higher-spending customer base to a lower-spending one and credits the discount with the difference — while the discount is actually quietly giving away margin.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Correct for the non-random assignment using the logged propensity — each session's probability, given its LTV score, of being shown the arm it actually got. Weighting each arm's revenue by the inverse of that propensity (a Hajek/self-normalized IPS estimator) estimates what each arm would earn across the full customer base, not just the LTV-skewed slice it was shown to. The honest gap doesn't just shrink — it flips sign: from a naive +$14 in the discount arm's favor to an honest -$1.79, meaning the discount arm actually earns slightly LESS revenue per session once LTV is held constant. Tell Farah: rolling the discount out everywhere would cost revenue, not grow it. The $14 gap in the logs was almost entirely which customers the bandit chose to discount, not the discount's real effect.
howToGetThere: Compute the naive gap: mean(revenue_per_session | discount) minus mean(revenue_per_session | standard) ≈ +$14.35.
Compare mean customer_ltv_score by arm: 58.6 (discount) vs. 42.9 (standard) — a large pre-existing gap, not caused by the pricing.
Name the mechanism: the logging policy's P(shown discount) rises with LTV score, so raw averages are confounded by who was targeted.
Compute the Hajek IPS estimate per arm: weight each arm's sessions by 1/propensity, take the weighted average revenue.
Compare: the IPS-corrected gap is ≈ -$1.79 — the naive +$14 'win' was entirely the LTV-targeting confound, and the true effect is a small revenue loss.

numbers.label: Mean LTV score, discount arm vs. standard
Share of traffic on the discount arm

teachingNote.lesson: A pricing bandit's raw average reward by arm only reflects the arm's true value if every arm was shown to a representative mix of customers — and a targeting heuristic layered onto a bandit (even a well-intentioned one, like protecting high-value customers) breaks that. When the assignment probability depends on the same variable that predicts the reward, a naive comparison is confounded exactly like an observational study, and the confound can be large enough to flip the sign of the conclusion, not just its size. Inverse-propensity weighting with the logged propensity is the standard correction — always check it before reading a bandit's raw arm averages as causal.
